fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, "Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah…" (Judges 11:29). After that, he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead. From there he advanced against the Ammonites.

I get why that one tempts you, friend. But this verse says the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. No angel is mentioned here (Judges 11:29). The Spirit comes, and then Jephthah passes through Gilead and Manasseh on his way to the Ammonites.

A deep sleep right before a battle? Jephthah would sleep through the whole thing, friend. The Bible does have a deep sleep from the LORD in another place, when He put Adam under (Genesis 2:21). Here it's different: the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, and then he advances against the Ammonites (Judges 11:29).

Yes, baker. The text says, "…there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing!" (Judges 11:34). She came out to meet him. I think this is where the story gets heavy, so let's take the next part gently.

I see why a servant sounds natural, friend, since a household has many people in it. But the text names his daughter as the one who comes out with tambourines and dancing (Judges 11:34). She's the one coming out to meet him.

The text never mentions a wife in this scene, baker. It says, "…there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing!" (Judges 11:34). Tambourines and dancing, and it's his daughter coming out to meet him. I think this is the moment the story turns.

Jephthah doesn't point to the elders here, friend. He says, "…I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." (Judges 11:35). His vow was made to the LORD (Judges 11:30), and in this verse he says nothing about who else heard it. I think this is a heavy moment for him.

The text doesn't mention an army in connection with the vow, baker. Jephthah made his vow "…to the LORD…" (Judges 11:30). And when he sees his daughter, he says, "…I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." (Judges 11:35). That's the reason he gives.
Sisters isn't the word in her request, baker. She asks to wander for two months "…through the mountains with my friends…" (Judges 11:37). Friends is the word the text gives.
The text says the opposite, friend. When she asks for two months, he answers, "Go," and he sent her away for two months (Judges 11:38). He grants her request.
That's right, baker. The text says she "…mourned her virginity upon the mountains." (Judges 11:38). She left with her friends to do it. I think we should let that sit for a moment.
